words.shortDefinition: Advanced Persistent Threat; state-sponsored actor with high capability, long-term patience, and specific target objectives.
words.simpleDefinition: An Advanced Persistent Threat is not a type of malware but a type of adversary: a well-resourced, typically nation-state-affiliated actor who conducts long-running targeted intrusion campaigns against specific organizations. 'Advanced' means sophisticated custom tooling; 'persistent' means they maintain access for months or years; 'threat' means they have both capability and intent.
words.longDefinition: The APT designation originated with U.S. Air Force analysts describing sophisticated intrusion campaigns against defense contractors around 2006. MITRE and intelligence community naming conventions track APTs by numbered designators (APT1, APT29, APT41) or vendor-specific names (Cozy Bear, Lazarus Group, Sandworm). Key characteristics: advanced — custom zero-day exploits, sophisticated malware like Stuxnet or SUNBURST, legitimate tool abuse (living off the land), supply chain compromise; persistent — maintain access for months to years, establish multiple redundant persistence mechanisms, evade detection through low-and-slow data collection; targeted — specific organizational objectives (steal IP, exfiltrate classified data, prepare for sabotage), they will retool after initial detection rather than abandoning the campaign. Defending against APTs requires capabilities beyond perimeter defense: assume breach posture, micro-segmentation to limit lateral movement, behavioral analytics and threat hunting to detect low-noise attacker activity, and privileged access management to limit blast radius when initial access is achieved. Nation-state APTs are the motivation for the most stringent Zero Trust architecture requirements.
words.connector: Think of an APT like a professional safecracker hired to steal specific valuables — they will spend months casing the building, disable specific security cameras, pick the right lock with custom tools, and leave no fingerprints, unlike opportunistic thieves who smash and grab.
words.techContext: After attributing the intrusion to an APT group, the incident response team shifted from eviction to observation mode for 72 hours to map all persistence mechanisms before simultaneously removing access — a standard countermeasure against APT retooling.
words.exampleSentence: The APT's three-month dwell time was enabled by a legitimate remote management tool already installed in the environment; behavioral analytics eventually flagged the unusual beacon timing pattern that signature-based detection had missed entirely.

words.shortDefinition: Expressing threat models in version-controlled code (e.g., pytm) so they evolve with the system and integrate with CI.
words.simpleDefinition: Threat-model-as-code applies the Infrastructure-as-Code principle to security threat modeling: instead of a static diagram in a Word document or Visio file, the threat model is expressed in code that is version-controlled, peer-reviewed, auto-generates DFDs and threat reports, and can be diffed when the architecture changes.
words.longDefinition: Traditional threat models suffer from the same problems as manual infrastructure management: they drift out of sync with the actual system, live in inaccessible formats (Visio, Word), are not peer-reviewed in code review, and do not produce actionable outputs automatically. Threat-model-as-code (TM-as-code) addresses this by expressing the system's components, data flows, trust boundaries, and threat actors in a domain-specific language that tooling can process. pytm (Python Threat Modeling) is the leading open-source implementation: developers define the system in Python code; pytm generates data flow diagrams, applies STRIDE categorization automatically, and produces a markdown or HTML threat report. The code lives in the repository alongside the application, is updated in the same PRs that change the architecture, is reviewed by security engineers during code review, and can be linted in CI to check for completeness (e.g., all data flows cross at least one trust boundary). The output is a living threat model that reflects the current state of the system rather than a historical snapshot. Microsoft's Threat Modeling Tool and OWASP's Threat Dragon provide GUI alternatives; pytm and similar code-first tools integrate better with developer workflows and CI/CD pipelines.
words.connector: Think of threat-model-as-code like a living blueprint that updates itself every time you make a change to the building — instead of a static floor plan in a filing cabinet that nobody looks at, it's a versioned document that stays current with every renovation.
words.techContext: We added a pytm threat model to the repository root; a CI job validates that all new data flows specify a protocol and cross at least one trust boundary — incomplete models fail the PR check before review.
words.exampleSentence: The threat-model-as-code diff in the PR immediately showed that adding the new data pipeline introduced an uncontrolled data flow from the external API to the internal database, surfacing a trust boundary violation that would have been missed in a manual review.

codeExample.code:
# pytm: threat model as Python code
from pytm import TM, Server, ExternalEntity, Dataflow, Boundary

tm = TM("Payment Service Threat Model")
tm.threatsFile = "pytm/threats.json"

internet = Boundary("Internet")
infra    = Boundary("Production VPC")

user      = ExternalEntity("User Browser",  inBoundary=internet)
api       = Server("Payment API",           inBoundary=infra, isHardened=True)
db        = Server("Postgres DB",           inBoundary=infra, isEncryptedAtRest=True)

Dataflow(user, api, "HTTPS payment request",  protocol="HTTPS", isEncrypted=True)
Dataflow(api,  db,  "SQL query",              protocol="TLS",   isEncrypted=True)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    tm.process()   # generates DFD + STRIDE threat report

words.etymology: Threat model (structured security analysis of a system's risks) + as-code (applying version-control and automation principles); the phrase mirrors 'infrastructure-as-code' and emerged alongside DevSecOps practices circa 2019.

words.shortDefinition: NIST's authoritative Zero Trust Architecture publication defining ZTA tenets, components, and deployment models.
words.simpleDefinition: NIST SP 800-207, published in August 2020, is the authoritative U.S. government definition of Zero Trust Architecture. It defines ZTA's three core tenets (verify explicitly, use least privilege, assume breach), the logical components of a ZTA (Policy Decision Point, Policy Enforcement Point), and three deployment models. It is the reference document for any serious ZTA implementation.
words.longDefinition: NIST Special Publication 800-207, 'Zero Trust Architecture,' was published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in August 2020 following a three-year development process including public comment periods. It is the most authoritative vendor-neutral specification of ZTA. The document defines ZTA's seven foundational tenets: (1) treat all resources as if on an untrusted network; (2) grant access per-session based on dynamic policy; (3) verify identity for all communications; (4) use dynamic policy incorporating behavioral signals; (5) monitor and measure integrity and security posture of all assets; (6) enforce strong authentication and authorization dynamically; (7) collect information to improve security posture. The logical architecture defines the Policy Decision Point (PDP, which evaluates access requests against policy and trust signals) and Policy Enforcement Point (PEP, which intercepts requests and enforces PDP decisions). Three ZTA deployment models: identity-governed (IdP as PDP), micro-segmented networks (SDN-enforced), and network infrastructure/SDP (software-defined perimeter). NIST 800-207A (2023) extends the guidance to multi-cloud environments. Executive Order 14028 (2021) directed federal agencies to develop ZTA migration plans based on NIST 800-207.
words.connector: Think of NIST SP 800-207 like a building code for Zero Trust — it doesn't tell you which specific products to buy, but it defines the required structural properties that any ZTA implementation must satisfy.
words.techContext: Our ZTA architecture review board uses NIST 800-207's seven tenets as a checklist — each proposed security control must be mapped to at least one tenet before it is included in the ZTA roadmap.
words.exampleSentence: The federal contractor's ZTA compliance audit required demonstrating that their Policy Decision Point evaluated all seven NIST 800-207 tenets, including dynamic device posture and behavioral signals beyond simple identity verification.
words.etymology: NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) + SP (Special Publication) + 800-207 (publication number in the 800 computer security series); published August 2020 as the authoritative federal ZTA specification.

words.shortDefinition: Module Lattice Digital Signature Algorithm (formerly Dilithium); NIST-standardized post-quantum signature scheme.
words.simpleDefinition: ML-DSA is NIST's post-quantum replacement for ECDSA and RSA signing. Published as FIPS 204 in August 2024 (formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium), it uses lattice mathematics to produce digital signatures that remain secure against quantum computers. It is the recommended algorithm for code signing, certificate issuance, and authentication in post-quantum systems.
words.longDefinition: ML-DSA (Module Lattice Digital Signature Algorithm), standardized as FIPS 204 in August 2024, was formerly known as CRYSTALS-Dilithium. It is based on the hardness of the Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) and Module Short Integer Solution (MSIS) problems — both believed to be resistant to quantum attacks including Shor's algorithm. As a digital signature algorithm it replaces ECDSA (P-256, P-384) and RSA signing in contexts where long-term security matters: code signing (signatures on software releases that must be verifiable years later), certificate authorities (root CA certificates with 20-year lifetimes), and any authentication token or document with a long validity window. ML-DSA comes in three security levels: ML-DSA-44 (category 2, ~AES-128 pre-quantum, category 1 post-quantum), ML-DSA-65 (category 3), and ML-DSA-87 (category 5). Key sizes are larger than ECDSA: an ML-DSA-65 public key is 1952 bytes versus 64 bytes for P-256. Signature sizes are also larger (3293 bytes for ML-DSA-65 vs. 64 bytes for ECDSA). This overhead is significant for TLS certificates and protocols where signature size matters; hybrid schemes (ECDSA + ML-DSA) are used during the transition period. NIST's companion standard SLH-DSA (FIPS 205, formerly SPHINCS+) provides a hash-based alternative with a more conservative security argument at the cost of larger signatures.
words.connector: Think of ML-DSA like a wax seal made from a new material that quantum computers cannot replicate — the seal looks different and is slightly larger than the old one, but it provides the same authentication guarantee that your signature is genuine.
words.techContext: Our code-signing pipeline was updated to produce both an ECDSA P-256 signature (for current verifiers) and an ML-DSA-65 signature (for future quantum-resistant verification) on every release artifact, stored alongside the binary.
words.exampleSentence: After migrating code signing to ML-DSA-65, release artifacts now carry signatures that will remain verifiable and unforgeable even if a cryptographically relevant quantum computer becomes available before those artifacts are retired.
